title: Cups versus eggs: capacity and size
intuition: This carton has cups for 24 eggs but holds 21. The cups are the capacity: storage the ArrayList has set aside. The eggs are the size(): the elements actually in the list, at indexes 0 to 20 — an empty cup is not an element, so get(21) fails even though there is room. When a 25th egg arrives, ArrayList fetches a bigger carton and moves every egg across for you; with a plain array you would have to do that yourself.
alt: A clear plastic carton for 24 eggs lying open on a wooden floor, holding 21 brown eggs with three empty cups at the front
caption: Room for 24, holding 21.

title: Slide a book in
intuition: Push a new book in between two others and every book to its right slides along one place. That is add(i, x): the new element takes index i and every later element's index goes up by one. Swapping one book for another moves nothing else — that is set(i, x). You can only take down a book that is there (positions 0 to size()−1), but you may add one at position size(), the very end. Where it breaks: you shove a row of books in one push, but the list moves each element separately, so inserting near the front of a long list is real work.
alt: A tightly packed shelf of hardback books of different heights and colours, editions of Aristotle's Metaphysics and Physics
caption: Make room, and everything to the right moves.

title: Seat position or seat number?
intuition: Every seat here has two numbers: its position in the row, counted from 0 at the left, and the number painted on it. In the second row from the front (219, 217, 215, 213…), position 1 holds the seat painted 217. On an ArrayList<Integer>, remove(1) means “the seat at position 1”, while remove(Integer.valueOf(211)) means “the seat with 211 painted on it”, wherever it is. Java chooses between them from the argument's type: a plain int is a position, an Integer is a value.
alt: Rows of light-blue stadium seats, each with a number painted on it; the second row from the front reads 219, 217, 215, 213, 211, 209
caption: Position 1 is not seat 1.
credit_html: Photo: Yann Duarte from Vitória, Brasil, 2010 · CC BY 2.0

title: The seat that slid past you
intuition: Walk along the front row removing every yellow seat, with everything to its right sliding one place left to close the gap (real seats are bolted down; a list's elements are not). At 21 you find yellow and remove it, so yellow 22 slides into the place you have just checked; you step on and find 23, and 22 is never looked at. That is what removing inside a forward loop over indexes does to two neighbouring matches. Walk from the right-hand end instead, let an Iterator do the removing, or copy the seats you keep into a new list.
alt: Numbered folding stadium seats in white, yellow, blue and red; in the front row seats 21 and 22 are both yellow, between a white 20 and a blue 23
caption: Remove 21, and 22 slides into the place you just checked.
credit_html: Photo: Katy Warner from Orlando, FL, USA, 2008 · CC BY-SA 2.0

title: Each clue points to the next
intuition: Each clue in a treasure hunt holds a small prize and says where the next clue is — this one leads to clue #3. That is a linked-list node: one value plus a link to the next node, and the nodes can sit anywhere. To reach clue 5 you cannot jump there; you start at the first clue and follow every link, which is why reaching index i in a LinkedList means walking. Once you are standing at the right clue, adding a new one only means rewriting one note — nothing else has to shift. Where it breaks: Java's LinkedList nodes also point back to the previous node, so it can be walked from either end.
alt: A handwritten treasure-hunt note propped beside a wrapped sweet, reading “A lantern named Jack will light the way to clue #3!”, with a glowing jack-o'-lantern blurred in front
caption: A value, and the way to the next one.

title: Join at the back, leave from the front
intuition: People join at the back, where the sign says ENTER HERE, and board at the front, so whoever has waited longest gets on first: first in, first out. A queue only ever uses its two ends, which is why a LinkedList or Python's collections.deque suits it. Taking the first element out of an ArrayList or Python list is like making everyone in this line step forward one place each time the bus takes a passenger. Where it breaks: in a real line people do step forward; in a deque or linked list nothing moves — only the record of who is at the front changes.
alt: A line of people waiting inside a chain barrier to board a shuttle bus at Grand Canyon; an ENTER HERE sign marks the back of the line
caption: First in, first out.

title: One jar design, many labels
intuition: Every jar on this shelf is made to the same design; only the label changes. Box<T> is the design and the type argument is the label: Box<String>, ArrayList<Book>. Because the label is part of the type, the compiler refuses to put the wrong thing in, and you know exactly what comes out without checking. Where it breaks: a paper label cannot stop anyone pouring in the wrong powder, but the compiler does stop you — and the label must name a class, so it is Integer, not int.
alt: A row of identical amber glass apothecary jars with stoppers on a glass shelf, each with an ornate paper label naming a different chemical
caption: The same jar; the label says what goes in.

title: Built to the standard, not the appliance
intuition: This power point does not care whether a kettle, a lamp or a phone charger is plugged in, as long as the plug has the standard shape. A method whose parameter is List<Integer> is the socket: an ArrayList or a LinkedList both fit, because the method uses only the operations every List promises. One thing does not follow: a List<Integer> is not a List<Number>. If it were, code holding it as a list of Numbers could add a Double to it — like pouring rice into the sugar jar because both are “food”.
alt: A white Australian double power point on a wall, with two switches and two three-pin sockets
caption: Any plug of the standard shape fits.
